articles.title: Jolly Josh Christmas Ball sells out as Rochdale businesses urged to help
articles.excerpt: The Castleton charity is asking businesses to sponsor a table for £50 or donate raffle and auction prizes ahead of its December ball at Rochdale Town Hall.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale charity Jolly Josh has filled the guest tables for its Jolly Jingle Christmas Ball and is now asking local businesses to help turn a full room into vital funding for families.

The ball takes place at Rochdale Town Hall on Friday 11 December at 7pm. With guest places filled, the charity is inviting businesses across Rochdale and Greater Manchester to sponsor tables for £50, donate raffle or auction prizes, or discuss other ways to support the evening.

A contribution does not have to be extravagant. Vouchers, meals, products, experiences and services can all help boost the fundraising total.

Based at Ensor Mill on Queensway in Castleton, Jolly Josh says it supports more than 300 families of children and young people with complex medical needs, physical disabilities, life limiting conditions, and profound and multiple learning disabilities.

Its purpose built centre offers hydrotherapy, rebound therapy, sensory activities, youth social groups, accessible after school provision and support for parents and carers.

The charity says it receives no regular government funding, making grants, donations, community fundraising and business support essential to keeping its services running.

Rose Hutchings, Lead Fundraiser at Jolly Josh, said:

“We’ve been absolutely delighted by the response to this year’s Jolly Jingle Ball and to see the tables fill. What we’d really love now is for the wider Rochdale business community to help us make the night as successful as possible for our families.

“A £50 table sponsorship or a donated raffle or auction prize might feel like a relatively small contribution to a business, but when lots of local organisations get behind us those contributions quickly add up.

“Jolly Josh doesn’t receive regular government funding, so fundraising and community support genuinely help us continue providing a safe, accessible place where children and young people with complex needs and their families can connect, access opportunities and feel part of a community.”

The appeal comes as demand for the charity’s specialist services continues to grow. Jolly Josh says its hydrotherapy provision has previously run at least 42 sessions a week and experienced waiting lists, with strong demand for other services too.

Businesses interested in a £50 table sponsorship, donating a raffle or auction prize, or offering other event support can email Rose Hutchings at rose@jollyjosh.co.uk or call 01706 399141.

Further information about Jolly Josh, registered charity number 1178116, is available at https://jollyjosh.co.uk/

Source: Jolly Josh press release supplied to Rochdale Daily.

articles.title: Young people inspire £85,000–£100,000 Castleton pump track proposal
articles.excerpt: A site beside the yellow play park on Manchester Road is being explored for a Castleton bike track, with young people helping shape the idea. Funding and approvals remain outstanding.
articles.content_html:
A new pump track costing an estimated £85,000 to £100,000 is being explored for Castleton after local young people asked for somewhere closer to home to ride their bikes.

Councillor Dave Jones said an area beside the yellow play park on Manchester Road had emerged as a promising potential location following discussions with council officers and youth workers.

The proposal remains at an early stage. No funding or final site approval has been announced, and there is no confirmed construction timetable.

In an update shared with Rochdale Daily, Cllr Jones described a positive meeting with Environmental Management, township officer Caroline and Jasmin from the Youth Work Team to discuss the concept.

Several possible locations were considered. According to the councillor, young people suggested the Manchester Road site because it feels safe. Its existing play area and car park could also make it convenient for families with children of different ages.

The idea is for younger children to use the playground while older children and teenagers could enjoy a nearby bike track, bringing different activities together in one central location.

Cllr Jones said those at the meeting supported involving young people in the design process. They also discussed whether contractors could explain how the track is built and explore suitable opportunities for young people to participate.

A bike repair hub was another suggestion. Local young people have spoken about their interest in repairing bicycles and sharing those skills with others. Secure bike storage lockers were also raised during the discussions.

The councillor said some young people currently travel to tracks elsewhere in the borough, including Littleborough, and expressed concern about the busy roads those journeys can involve. He believes a Castleton facility could offer a more convenient option and reassurance for families.

Funding is the main obstacle. Cllr Jones put the initial estimated cost at between £85,000 and £100,000 and said several processes and approvals would need to be completed before any scheme could proceed.

Council officers are now exploring possible funding sources, according to his update. A further meeting is planned to discuss potential designs and ensure any future proposal reflects what local young people want.

Cllr Jones also thanked Keane, the young person who first approached him with the idea, and praised young residents for taking an active role in improving their community.

He cautioned: “It's important to stress that projects like this take time, and there is still a long way to go.”

The potential location, repair hub, storage lockers and construction involvement are all ideas under discussion rather than confirmed features of an approved scheme.

Would your family use a pump track in Castleton, and what would you like a future design to include? Share your views in the comments.

articles.title: Jolly Josh welcomes Rochdale families with inclusive play, music and activity sessions
articles.excerpt: The Castleton charity is reaching out to families caring for children and young people with complex medical needs and physical disabilities, with weekly sessions and bookable activities.
articles.content_html:
Rochdale charity Jolly Josh is reaching out to families caring for children and young people with complex medical needs and physical disabilities, with a programme of inclusive activities and support.

Based at 2 Ensor Mill in Castleton, Rochdale, OL11 2NU, the centre welcomes children and young adults aged from birth to 19.

The charity says finding activities where a child is welcomed, understood and supported can be difficult, and wants more parents, carers, relatives and professionals to know what is available.

Its programme includes music and signing, themed play sessions, an after-school club, a youth group and activities that families can book directly with the centre.

Weekly sessions

Sing And Sign runs every Wednesday from 10.30am to 12.30pm, bringing together music, songs and signing to make communication fun.

Themed Stay And Play takes place every Tuesday and Saturday from 9.30am to 12.30pm. Sessions offer activities, friendship and a different theme each week.

Sensory Touch And Music runs every Thursday from 10am to noon, offering a relaxing sensory session.

The After School Club takes place every Wednesday from 4pm to 7pm, with inclusive activities and a light tea offered for every child.

The Youth Group meets every Thursday from 5pm to 8pm, giving young people a welcoming space to socialise, take part in activities and build friendships.

Activities available to book

Hydrotherapy sessions can be booked for families or with the centre’s Hydro Lead.

Private sound bath sessions are also available by contacting the centre, offering an opportunity to take time out of a busy schedule.

Rebound Therapy provides supported movement and sensory experiences using a trampoline, with sessions bookable through the centre.

How to get in touch

Parents, carers, family members and professionals supporting a child with complex medical needs are invited to contact Jolly Josh to learn more about its sessions.

Call 01706 399141, email sarah@jollyjosh.co.uk or visit https://jollyjosh.co.uk/

The centre asks anyone planning to visit to contact the team first so an appointment can be arranged.

Families can contact the centre to discuss which sessions suit their child and ask about booking, availability and charges.

The charity is also encouraging people to share its appeal with families who may not yet know about the support available.

Source: Jolly Josh session information supplied to Rochdale Daily; centre details confirmed through https://jollyjosh.co.uk/

articles.title: Castleton Sidings brings 191 homes, with discounted ownership and rail land in the package
articles.excerpt: Hawks View is a 191-home development on the former Castleton Sidings site. Kellen’s current partnership page identifies 162 market homes, ten First Homes and 19 affordable homes with Mosscare St Vincent. The rental/ownership split within those 19 remains unspecified.
articles.content_html:
Hawks View is a 191-home development on the former Castleton Sidings site. Kellen’s current partnership page identifies 162 market homes, ten First Homes and 19 affordable homes with Mosscare St Vincent. The rental/ownership split within those 19 remains unspecified.

The ten First Homes are discounted ownership, not social-rented homes. The project therefore has 29 homes in affordable categories, approximately 15.2% of the total, without establishing how many will be socially rented. Earlier references to a different provider should not override the current partnership schedule.

The scheme includes open space and land intended to support East Lancashire Railway expansion and future tram-train infrastructure. Reserving or gifting land does not establish the funding or opening date of a passenger service. Reporting at approval also identified education and rugby-club contributions, which should be checked against the executed agreement.

Current advertised prices and the discounted announcement price are set out below. They should not be used as the rent or purchase cost of the separate 19-home MSV package.

No verified site-specific adverse legal finding was established in this review. That is a statement about the evidence examined, not a guarantee about every corporate or customer dispute. Completed and remaining homes must be separated when calculating future supply.

Location: Heywood Road, Castleton; marketed as Hawks View

Planning stage: Consent secured and homes released for sale

Homes: 191 total; 29 described as affordable

Let or for sale: 162 market sale; 10 First Homes; 19 MSV affordable homes, detailed tenure split unconfirmed

Land: Former railway sidings: brownfield housing site, with a retained ecology/open-space area

Final planning agreement: The council’s 2024/25 Infrastructure Funding Statement lists an agreement entered into for 23/00431/HYBR. The complete executed deed and any variations were not retrieved; reporting describes £450,000 education and £300,000 rugby contributions.

Exact rents / prices: Kellen’s live sales page advertises market homes from £297,995. Its show-home announcement advertised discounted two-bedroom homes from £180,600. The latter is an announcement price, not a confirmed available plot quotation. Exact MSV rents, shared-ownership costs and charges are not disclosed in the reviewed sources.

Affordable breakdown: Kellen’s partnership page: 162 open-market homes, 10 First Homes, 19 affordable homes with Mosscare St Vincent; total 191. The 19-home rental/ownership split is not specified. This precise schedule supersedes ambiguous publicity.

Funded school capacity: £450,000 education contribution is reported. No site-linked receipt/spend record, named funded school project, additional places or opening date verified. The borough-wide funding statement cannot establish those details.

Funded healthcare capacity: No site-specific funded NHS expansion, additional staffed appointment capacity or delivery date was established from the accessible council/government records reviewed. Proximity to a surgery is not a capacity assessment.

Funded transport capacity: Railway/tram-train land and open space feature in the scheme. No funded passenger-service opening or complete transport-capacity package verified.

The outstanding details identified above are not yet available to Rochdale Daily. This article will be updated when the information becomes available.

articles.title: Trows Farm’s 445 market homes put the spotlight on off-site affordable housing
articles.excerpt: The approved Trows Farm scheme is reported as 445 market homes, with an initial £3.75 million contribution towards affordable housing rather than affordable properties within the development. The proposal is smaller than the strategic allocation and those two totals must not be added together.
articles.content_html:
The approved Trows Farm scheme is reported as 445 market homes, with an initial £3.75 million contribution towards affordable housing rather than affordable properties within the development. The proposal is smaller than the strategic allocation and those two totals must not be added together.

Approval reporting describes education, sports and a £190,000 TfGM contribution linked to changes in viability during delivery. The executed agreement is needed to establish which payments are unconditional, which depend on a review and when each becomes payable.

An earlier committee decision was deferred over emergency access, with residents also raising traffic, school and healthcare concerns. Subsequent approval does not erase those questions: it makes the final access conditions and their implementation the documents residents need to examine.

In August 2026 the Environment Agency advertised a settlement-tank permit application from BDW Trading, involving discharge to a tributary of Trub Brook via a lake. This is a regulatory application, not evidence of unlawful pollution, and the consultation deadline has passed.

Barratt Redrow joined the CMA’s 2025 commitments settlement, closed without an infringement finding. This does not establish a breach at the local development.

Location: Cowm Top Lane, Castleton

Planning stage: Approval reported in March 2025; environmental permit application published August 2026

Homes: 445 detailed scheme homes; distinct from the approximately 550-home strategic allocation

Let or for sale: Reported 100% market housing; affordable housing supported through an initial cash contribution

Land: Undulating greenfield land

Final planning agreement: The executed Section 106 deed, complete schedules, payment triggers and later variations were not verified. This is an evidence gap, not a claim that no agreement exists.

Exact rents / prices: No exact plot-price schedule established in the reviewed sources; no on-site affordable rent is promised by the reported 100% market scheme.

Affordable breakdown: 445 market homes reported. An initial £3.75 million off-site affordable contribution is reported; the number, location, tenure and delivery dates of homes it will fund are not established.

Funded school capacity: Education contributions are reported, but the final secured amount, payment triggers and school project/capacity were not verified.

Funded healthcare capacity: No site-specific funded NHS expansion, additional staffed appointment capacity or delivery date was established from the accessible council/government records reviewed. Proximity to a surgery is not a capacity assessment.

Funded transport capacity: A £190,000 TfGM contribution is reported alongside viability-linked obligations. The executed deed is needed to establish unconditional versus review-dependent sums. Final emergency-access delivery and funded extra public-transport capacity are not verified.

The outstanding details identified above are not yet available to Rochdale Daily. This article will be updated when the information becomes available.

articles.title: Trub Farm’s 158 affordable homes could offer Castleton both rented homes and ownership
articles.excerpt: Trub Farm is intended to deliver 158 affordable homes through MCI Developments and Legal & General Affordable Homes. Reported plans comprise 48 apartments and 110 houses, with homes for social rent and shared ownership.
articles.content_html:
Trub Farm is intended to deliver 158 affordable homes through MCI Developments and Legal & General Affordable Homes. Reported plans comprise 48 apartments and 110 houses, with homes for social rent and shared ownership.

The distinction between those tenures is crucial. Social rent is a rental product; shared ownership involves buying a share and meeting additional ongoing costs. Until the final schedule is available, the total should not be described as 158 social-rented homes.

The reporting contains a date discrepancy. An August 2025 article records a committee vote in favour, subject to a legal agreement, while an August 2026 deal article describes approval the previous month. The decision notice and agreement are needed to reconcile a committee resolution with formal permission.

The council committee report identifies open grassland within the urban boundary, adjoining Green Belt rather than simply being described as a Green Belt farm. Its consultation responses require mitigation, but do not establish an already funded expansion in school or GP capacity.

The regulator’s 2026 casework review records strong inspection grades for L&G Affordable Homes and oversight of third-party repairs providers. That provides relevant landlord context, rather than a promise about homes not yet occupied. If delivered, Trub Farm would directly expand affordable options, but exact rents, shares and service charges remain essential missing information.

Location: Off Manchester Road, Castleton

Planning stage: Committee approval reported in 2025; MCI/L&G agreement reported August 2026

Homes: 158: 48 apartments and 110 houses

Let or for sale: Social rent and shared ownership; precise split and charges unconfirmed

Land: Open grassland within the Defined Urban Area; Green Belt adjoins the west and south

Final planning agreement: The executed Section 106 deed, complete schedules, payment triggers and later variations were not verified. This is an evidence gap, not a claim that no agreement exists.

Exact rents / prices: No exact future rent, sale price, service charge or estate-charge schedule was established from the council/government material reviewed; no reliable scheme-specific current quotation was identified.

Affordable breakdown: 158 affordable homes. Committee report: 24 one-bedroom and 24 two-bedroom flats; 56 two-bedroom, 46 three-bedroom and eight four-bedroom houses. These are dwelling sizes, not tenure counts. The report defers the final tenure mix to approval of an Affordable Housing Scheme.

Funded school capacity: The committee report requests primary and secondary education contributions; the final amounts, receipts and funded additional places were not established.

Funded healthcare capacity: No site-specific funded NHS expansion, additional staffed appointment capacity or delivery date was established from the accessible council/government records reviewed. Proximity to a surgery is not a capacity assessment.

Funded transport capacity: Highways raised no objection subject to measures including a self-enforcing 20mph layout, travel plan, construction management and bridge survey. These conditions do not establish additional funded bus/rail capacity.

The outstanding details identified above are not yet available to Rochdale Daily. This article will be updated when the information becomes available.

Research checked 14 October 2026. Advertised prices are snapshots, not achieved sale prices.

articles.title: Loombrook Meadows: 302 new homes coming to Castleton - what we know so far
articles.excerpt: Barratt Homes has broken ground on a 302-home development at Cowm Top Lane, with two, three and four bedroom houses expected to go on sale from autumn. What's being built, who it's for, and the affordability question.
articles.content_html:
A brand new development of two, three and four bedroom homes is coming to Castleton - and buyers are already being invited to register their interest.

Loombrook Meadows, being built by Barratt Homes on Cowm Top Lane, will deliver 302 new homes on the southern edge of the borough. Construction began in early June, and the developer expects the first properties to be available to reserve from autumn 2026.

Barratt says the homes will be built with a stone effect intended to match the character of the local area, using modern construction methods designed to make them more energy efficient and cheaper to run. The development is expected to support around 604 jobs during construction.

The developer is pitching the site at young professionals, first-time buyers and growing families, pointing to Castleton railway station, the M62 and local schools and shops on the doorstep. Rhys Nicholson, managing director at Barratt Homes Manchester, said the scheme had already seen strong interest from those groups and encouraged anyone interested to register for updates on the homes available later this year.

How affordable will they be?

Prices for Loombrook Meadows have not yet been released. As a guide, Barratt's other current developments in the wider area list two to four bedroom homes from around £198,000 up to £459,000, and the company promotes schemes such as reduced-rate mortgage products and assisted moves for buyers with a home to sell. Until the first releases are priced, it is impossible to say where Loombrook Meadows will sit within that range, or how many of the 302 homes will be classed as affordable housing - a figure usually settled through the planning process. Rochdale Daily has asked for details of the affordable housing provision and will update this article when they are confirmed.

The bigger picture

The development lands in the middle of a familiar local argument. Rochdale, like most of Greater Manchester, does not have enough homes: demand for social housing far outstrips supply, private rents have climbed steeply, and many working households find themselves priced out of buying altogether. New building on this scale is one of the few levers that can ease that pressure.

At the same time, large housing schemes in and around Castleton routinely draw concern from existing residents about traffic on already busy roads, pressure on GP surgeries and school places, and the loss of open land. Those arguments were aired when the Cowm Top site went through planning, and they will not disappear now the diggers have arrived.

What is not in dispute is the need. A borough of around 220,000 people cannot house its next generation in its existing stock, and every credible plan for Rochdale's future involves building substantially more homes. The test for Loombrook Meadows will be whether the homes that emerge are ones ordinary Rochdale families can actually afford - and whether the infrastructure around them keeps pace.

Buyers can register their interest through the Barratt Homes website.
articles.legal_disclaimer: Details of the development are based on information published by Barratt Homes and local reporting of the start of construction. Prices, tenure mix and affordable housing figures had not been published at the time of writing and this article will be updated when they are confirmed.

articles.title: Comment: Government changes to local planning risk shutting residents out
articles.excerpt: From October 2026, most planning applications will be decided by officers with no route to a public committee hearing. Castleton councillor David Jones argues the reforms trade local democracy for speed.
articles.content_html:
This is a comment article by Councillor David Jones (Reform UK, Castleton), a member of Rochdale Borough Council's Planning Committee. The views expressed are his own.

As a member of Rochdale Council's Planning Committee, I want to make residents aware of significant changes being introduced by the Labour Government to the way planning applications are decided.

From 31 October 2026, a new national system will divide planning applications into two schedules.

Schedule 1 applications must be decided by planning officers, with no option for them to be brought before the Planning Committee. This will include householder applications, minor commercial developments and some residential developments of up to nine homes. Regardless of the level of local concern, these applications will not receive a public decision by elected members.

For Schedule 2 applications, the starting assumption will also be that they are decided by officers. They will only come before the Planning Committee if they meet a test relating to significant local or planning issues, and both a nominated senior planning officer and the chair of the Planning Committee agree that committee consideration is warranted. If they cannot agree, the application will remain with officers.

Perhaps most concerningly, ward councillors will lose the ability to call a planning application before the committee. Councils will also be unable to guarantee committee consideration simply because an application has attracted a large number of objections.

Residents will still be able to submit comments and objections, and relevant planning concerns must still be considered. However, making an objection is not the same as having the application examined and debated publicly by elected councillors.

HMOs are a major concern for many Castleton residents. Where an HMO proposal requires planning permission, residents may submit objections, but neither they nor their ward councillor will be able to guarantee that it receives a public committee hearing. Instead, that decision will rest with a senior officer and the committee chair.

The Government says these changes will provide greater consistency and allow committees to concentrate on the most significant developments.

I understand the need for an efficient planning system, but I do not believe efficiency should come at the expense of local democracy.

A planning application that appears "minor" on paper can have a major impact on the people living beside it. Local circumstances cannot always be understood through a national classification or an officer's written report.

In my view, removing councillors' call-in powers takes away an important democratic safeguard. It weakens the ability of elected representatives to ensure that residents' legitimate concerns are heard and debated publicly.

This is not about councillors ignoring planning law or blocking development without proper grounds. It is about retaining openness, accountability and meaningful local representation in decisions that can permanently affect our neighbourhoods.

I will continue to speak up for Castleton residents and raise my concerns about any change that further distances local people from decisions affecting where they live.

Greater consistency should not mean less democracy, and faster decisions should not mean residents having less of a say.
articles.legal_disclaimer: This is a comment article written by an elected councillor. The views expressed are those of the author and not of Rochdale Daily. Details of the national scheme of delegation are as described by the author and readers should consult official government guidance for the definitive position.
